prompt: pip-audit said "Found 6 known vulnerabilities" in requests 2.31.0. How many distinct advisories were there?
hint: Read the ID column, not the count.

prompt: What does pip-audit check when it is run with no -r?

choices.text: The requirements files under the current directory
choices.why: It reads a file only when -r names one.

choices.text: The environment it is installed in
choices.why: Right. Here, lesson 6's virtual environment, pip included.

choices.text: The packages Ubuntu installed with apt
choices.why: apt's packages are not Python distributions it can see.

choices.text: The Python files of the current project
choices.why: SCA never reads your own code.

prompt: The audit of lesson 6's virtual environment found something. What was it?

choices.text: Locust 2.46.7, the load generator
choices.why: Locust and everything under it came back clean.

choices.text: pip-audit itself, an outdated release
choices.why: pip-audit 2.10.1 had no advisory.

choices.text: pip 24.0, the version venv installed
choices.why: Right. Six advisories, fixed by upgrading pip.

choices.text: requests 2.31.0 from the audit project
choices.why: requests was never installed in the venv; -r audits it in a temporary one.

prompt: Match each name to what it is.
How does a CVSS environmental score differ from the base score an advisory publishes?

choices.text: It is the base score after the fix is installed
choices.why: After the fix there is no finding to score.

choices.text: It fits the flaw to your own system
choices.why: Right. Worked out by the people who run it.

choices.text: It is published later, once exploits are seen
choices.why: That describes threat information, not your environment.

choices.text: It is the average of the scores of all databases
choices.why: No average is involved; the context is.

prompt: PYSEC-2026-2275 is real for requests 2.31.0, and notify.py never calls extract_zipped_paths(). How is it classified?
hint: Right about the library, or wrong about the system?

choices.text: A false positive, to be deleted from the report
choices.why: The finding is true about the installed version.

choices.text: A false negative of the scanner
choices.why: A false negative is a flaw the scanner missed.

choices.text: A true positive with a low priority
choices.why: Right. True about the library, unreachable from this code today.

choices.text: A critical finding, since its base score decides
choices.why: The base score starts triage; context finishes it.

prompt: Why does the lesson say to search for a finding by its CVE?
hint: Which id is the same in every report?

choices.text: It is the same id in all databases
choices.why: Right. It joins this report to a colleague's triage of another.

choices.text: CVE pages carry the fix as a patch to apply
choices.why: The fix is a version of the library, named in the advisory.

choices.text: --ignore-vuln is built to take CVE ids
choices.why: audit.sh ignored a PYSEC id.

choices.text: Its year says how old the flaw is in your code
choices.why: That is how long the version has been pinned.

prompt: Whether a library's flaw can be triggered from your own code is the question of whether it is ___.
hint: The grep was looking for it.

prompt: The grep for verify=False, trust_env and extract_zipped_paths found nothing in notify.py. Why is that a first answer and not a proof?
hint: What would a grep not see?

choices.text: grep reads only the first hundred lines of a file
choices.why: It reads the whole file.

choices.text: A call through a variable or another library
choices.why: Right. A name in a string, or code in a dependency, hides from a text search.

choices.text: The advisories name the wrong function
choices.why: The description is the vendor's own and names it exactly.

choices.text: grep exits with 1, which means it failed to run
choices.why: Exit 1 from grep means no match; 2 would be an error.

prompt: A pipeline runs pip-audit --ignore-vuln PYSEC-2026-2275, with no comment. What is missing for it to be an accepted risk?

choices.text: A CVSS score above 7
choices.why: Acceptance does not need a score above anything.

choices.text: The fixed version's number
choices.why: Useful, but the acceptance is about people and time.

choices.text: The reason, an owner and an end date
choices.why: Right. Without them the flag only makes the report quiet.

choices.text: A second run with -f json
choices.why: The format changes nothing about the decision.

prompt: audit.sh accepted PYSEC-2026-2275 and still exited 1 against requests 2.31.0. Why?
hint: How many lines were ignored, and how many were left?

choices.text: The acceptance had already expired
choices.why: That was the second run, which stopped before pip-audit.

choices.text: The two other advisories were not accepted
choices.why: Right. Ignoring one says nothing about the rest.

choices.text: --ignore-vuln needs a CVE id to work
choices.why: It ignored two lines, the accepted advisory printed twice.

choices.text: audit.sh exits 1 whenever it ignores something
choices.why: After the fix it exited 0 with the same acceptance in it.

prompt: After the upgrade to requests 2.33.0, what should happen to the acceptance in audit.sh?
hint: It ignores an advisory that no longer appears.

choices.text: Leave it, it costs nothing
choices.why: It is a decision nobody checks any more.

choices.text: Extend its date by a year
choices.why: There is nothing left to accept.

choices.text: Take it out the same day
choices.why: Right. An acceptance that outlives its finding is checking nothing.

choices.text: Move it to the pip line
choices.why: pip's findings were fixed by upgrading, not accepted.

prompt: What does ZAP's baseline scan do to the site it is pointed at?

choices.text: Sends probing requests to the forms it finds
choices.why: That is the full scan's active rules.

choices.text: Crawls it briefly and reads the answers
choices.why: Right. Passive rules, nothing attacked.

choices.text: Reads its source code from the server
choices.why: DAST sees only HTTP answers.

choices.text: Audits its dependency list
choices.why: That is SCA, what pip-audit does.

prompt: A ZAP alert is High risk with Low confidence. What comes first?
hint: Risk is how bad; confidence is how sure.

choices.text: Block the release at once
choices.why: Nobody knows yet whether it is real.

choices.text: Mark it as a false positive
choices.why: Low confidence is not proof of a false one.

choices.text: Confirm it by hand on the URL it names
choices.why: Right. Then rate it in your context.

choices.text: Raise it to Critical to be safe
choices.why: Inflating ratings teaches everybody to ignore them.

prompt: One alert, a missing security header, has 50 instances. How many fixes does it need?

choices.text: Fifty, one per page
choices.why: The pages share the code that sends headers.

choices.text: One, in the code that sends the headers
choices.why: Right. One cause behind fifty instances.

choices.text: Zero: headers are a deployment matter
choices.why: Lesson 19 tested headers in the code.

choices.text: As many as the confidence says
choices.why: Confidence says how sure, not how many.

prompt: Put in order what happens to a dependency finding, from report to release.
items: collapse the duplicate lines into advisories
read each advisory's conditions and look for them in the code
rate it in your own context
fix it, or accept it with a reason, an owner and an end date
let the gate in the pipeline check the result

prompt: Lesson 1's rule is no finding rated high or critical left open at release. Which of these releases keep it? Choose every one.
hint: Open means neither fixed nor accepted.

choices.text: A critical finding removed by an upgrade before the release
choices.why: Right. Fixed is not open.

choices.text: A high finding accepted by its owner until a date, with the reason
choices.why: Right. Accepted with all four parts is not open.

choices.text: A medium finding still open, with a ticket
choices.why: Right. The rule speaks of high and critical.

choices.text: A high finding silenced with --ignore-vuln and no reason
choices.why: Ignored is not accepted: nobody owns it, nothing ends it.

choices.text: A critical finding nobody triaged because the report was long
choices.why: Untriaged and unfixed is open.

prompt: A colleague wants to point ZAP's full scan at the ticketing partner's public API, to check its headers before integrating. What is the right answer?

choices.text: Go ahead, since the API is public
choices.why: Public is not permission; probing it without consent is illegal.

choices.text: The baseline scan is fine, it attacks nothing
choices.why: Even a gentle scan of somebody else's system needs their written permission.

choices.text: Run it at night, when nobody is using it
choices.why: The hour changes nothing about authorisation.

choices.text: Not without the partner's written permission
choices.why: Right. Ask them, or scan your own staging only.
